lead: Threshold voltage VT is the gate-source voltage at which an nMOS surface flips into inversion. Part of that voltage bends the bands and empties the body; only the rest creates inversion charge. This chapter splits VT into its physical pieces and adds the body effect: when the source sits above the body, the depletion region holds more charge and VT rises. Circuit designers use this to size stacked transistors, estimate pass-transistor levels, and set SPICE models.
prereq: You need: accumulation, depletion and inversion from 1.1.

blocks.text: For an nMOS with a p-type body, start with zero gate voltage. The gate work function and the body differ, so a flat-band voltage VFB is needed just to make the bands flat. Fixed oxide charge Qox shifts it too: VFB = φMS − Qox/Cox. φMS is the gate-to-body work function difference in volts; Qox is fixed oxide charge per unit area in C/m²; Cox is oxide capacitance per unit area in F/m².

As gate voltage rises, holes are pushed away and a depletion region forms. At inversion onset the surface potential is 2φF. φF is the bulk Fermi potential: φF = (kT/q) ln(NA/ni). kT/q is thermal voltage, about 26 mV at 300 K; NA is acceptor doping in m⁻³; ni is intrinsic concentration in m⁻³. For NA = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³, φF ≈ 0.41 V and 2φF ≈ 0.82 V.

blocks.where: VT0 is threshold voltage with source tied to body, in V; VFB is flat-band voltage in V; φF is bulk Fermi potential in V; q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C is electron charge; εsi is silicon permittivity, about 1.04×10⁻¹⁰ F/m; NA is acceptor doping in m⁻³; Cox = εox/tox is oxide capacitance per unit area in F/m²; εox is oxide permittivity, about 3.45×10⁻¹¹ F/m; tox is oxide thickness in m.

blocks.text: The square-root term is depletion charge per unit area divided by Cox. It is the gate voltage spent on depletion charge before inversion charge appears. At threshold the inversion charge is still zero, so the gate supports band bending, depletion charge and flat-band shift only.

Tie the source to the body and VSB = 0. Raise the source above the body and the source-body junction is reverse biased. VSB is source voltage minus body voltage in volts. The depletion region widens, exposing more ionized acceptors, so depletion charge Qdep increases. The gate must supply more voltage before the surface reaches inversion. That is the body effect.

blocks.where: VT is threshold voltage at a given source-to-body voltage, in V; VT0 is threshold voltage with VSB = 0, in V; γ is body-effect coefficient in √V; φF is bulk Fermi potential in V; VSB is source-to-body voltage in V, positive for reverse bias in an nMOS.
γ is body-effect coefficient in √V; q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C; εsi is silicon permittivity in F/m; NA is acceptor doping in m⁻³; Cox is oxide capacitance per unit area in F/m². Typical γ is 0.1 to 0.5 √V.

blocks.text: For small VSB the rise is almost linear; for large VSB it grows slowly as √VSB. The formula assumes reverse bias, strong inversion and uniform body doping. It is an nMOS formula; a pMOS needs reversed signs. Body effect is zero when source and body are tied together. It matters for stacked and pass transistors, whose source can float above the body.
Temperature also shifts VT. As temperature rises, φF and depletion charge change, and VT falls by roughly 1 to 2 mV per °C. In SPICE Level 1 the numbers are carried by VTO, GAMMA, PHI and TOX.

sections.h3: Reading the curve and the numbers

blocks.text: The figure after Section 1 plots VT against VSB with VT0 = 0.45 V and 2φF = 0.82 V. At VSB = 1 V, γ = 0.21 √V gives VT ≈ 0.544 V; γ = 0.42 √V gives VT ≈ 0.636 V. At VSB = 3 V the same curves reach about 0.670 V and 0.891 V. The stronger coefficient does not change VT at VSB = 0; it changes how fast VT climbs.

items: Use VSB, not VBS, in the square root.
Keep NA in m⁻³ when you use q and εsi in SI units.
γ has units √V, so γ times a square-root voltage gives volts.

blocks.text: Most courses expect you to use the result and explain the mechanism. The phrase threshold voltage effects means body effect, temperature and short-channel changes. Short-channel changes belong to 1.6; leakage cost of a low VT belongs to 1.7.

figure.caption: Threshold voltage against source-to-body voltage for two body-effect coefficients, both starting from 0.45 V. At VSB = 1 V the larger coefficient has raised VT more; at VSB = 0 the curves meet.

spec.aria: Two curves of threshold voltage against source-to-body voltage starting from 0.45 V, the stronger body-effect coefficient giving the steeper rise.

examples.question: An nMOS has NA = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ and tox = 4 nm. Use εsi = 1.04×10⁻¹⁰ F/m, εox = 3.45×10⁻¹¹ F/m, q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, ni = 1.5×10¹⁰ cm⁻³, and kT/q = 0.026 V. (a) Find Cox, φF and γ. (b) Take VT0 = 0.45 V and find VT at VSB = 1 V.
steps: Convert doping: NA = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ × 10⁶ cm³/m³ = 10²³ m⁻³.
Oxide capacitance: Cox = εox/tox = 3.45×10⁻¹¹ F/m ÷ 4×10⁻⁹ m = 8.625×10⁻³ F/m².
Threshold: VT = VT0 + ΔVT = 0.45 V + 0.0939 V = 0.5439 V.
examples.answer: VT ≈ 0.544 V at VSB = 1 V; γ ≈ 0.2115 √V and Cox ≈ 8.625×10⁻³ F/m².
examples.check:
import math
q = 1.6e-19
eps_si = 1.04e-10
eps_ox = 3.45e-11
NA_cm3 = 1e17
NA = NA_cm3 * 1e6
tox = 4e-9
ni_cm3 = 1.5e10
kT_q = 0.026
Cox = eps_ox / tox
phi_F = kT_q * math.log(NA_cm3 / ni_cm3)
two_phi = 2 * phi_F
gamma = math.sqrt(2 * q * eps_si * NA) / Cox
VT0 = 0.45
VSB = 1.0
delta_VT = gamma * (math.sqrt(two_phi + VSB) - math.sqrt(two_phi))
VT = VT0 + delta_VT
print(f'{Cox:.6f}')
print(f'{phi_F:.4f}')
print(f'{two_phi:.4f}')
print(f'{gamma:.4f}')
print(f'{delta_VT:.4f}')
print(f'{VT:.4f}')

traps: VBS versus VSB: the body-effect formula needs VSB = VS − VB. Using VBS flips the sign and can make the threshold appear to fall under reverse bias.
γ is not dimensionless. It has units √V; a γ quoted in volts or V⁻¹ is wrong.
The formula uses 2φF, not φF. Using φF alone halves the band-bending term.
For SI calculation, convert NA from cm⁻³ to m⁻³. Mixing cm⁻³ with F/m and q gives an answer off by 10³ or worse.
Body effect is zero only when source and body are at the same potential. In a stack, the upper transistor can have VSB > 0 even though the lower one has VSB = 0.

quiz.q: Define threshold voltage VT for an nMOS transistor.
quiz.a: VT is the gate-source voltage at which the surface potential reaches 2φF and inversion charge just begins to form, with the source as reference.

quiz.q: Why does reverse body-source bias raise VT?
quiz.a: It widens the depletion region, adding depletion charge. The gate must support that extra charge before inversion, so threshold rises.

quiz.q: VT0 = 0.5 V, γ = 0.30 √V, 2φF = 0.80 V, VSB = 2 V. Find VT.
A student computes ΔVT with VBS = −1 V and gets a smaller VT. What went wrong?
quiz.a: The formula needs VSB, not VBS. For reverse bias VSB = +1 V, so VT should rise. A negative value under the square root is invalid for a reverse-biased nMOS.

quiz.q: What are the SI units of γ?
Why is the body effect absent in a transistor whose source is tied to the body?
quiz.a: Then VSB = 0, so √(2φF + VSB) − √(2φF) = 0 and ΔVT = 0.

quiz.q: VT falls by 1.5 mV/°C. How much does it fall when temperature rises by 50 °C?
In a two-input nMOS NAND stack, which transistor can show body effect when both inputs are high and the output is low?
quiz.a: The upper nMOS. Its source sits at the lower transistor's drain voltage above ground, so VSB > 0 if the body is grounded. The lower nMOS has source at ground and VSB = 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern compact models such as BSIM do not use this single square-root formula; they add doping profiles, short-channel terms and back-gate coefficients. FD-SOI and body-biasing research use the same idea: changing the body voltage changes VT and leakage. Search for BSIM4 threshold voltage parameters, body bias coefficient, and back-gate bias in FD-SOI if you want the industrial version.
